landing.eyebrow: Trade analytics built on your own tags
landing.panelNote: Illustration only — the numbers on this panel are made up.
landing.ctaNote: Free. All it needs is read-only exchange keys.
landing.heroTitle: Find your trading system and make it stable
landing.heroLede: Trade Play is not a journal for journaling's sake, and not a second terminal. It is a read on your trading: what repeats from trade to trade, and what it costs you. Trades arrive from the exchange on their own — you answer one question: why you entered.
landing.step1Title: Find what actually works for you
landing.step1Body: You tag why you entered a trade. The vocabulary is yours: setups named by someone else get abandoned within a week. Trade Play counts how each of those reasons ended and shows which setups actually make money, and which only look like they work.
landing.step2Title: Test it on your own data
landing.step2Body: Analytics compares a selection matching your conditions — tag, direction, instrument, hour of entry — against all your other trades. The question it answers is “what if I only traded like this?”, and the answer arrives before you put money behind it.
landing.step3Body: Edge Score measures not the size of the profit but how repeatable it is. Together with the equity curve, drawdown and profit factor it answers the real question: has the system become steadier or not.
landing.section_overview_body: The period in nine numbers, an equity curve with drawdown, open positions and the trade log. Time in position is counted separately for winners and losers — the gap between them honestly shows how you exit.
landing.section_tags_body: Your tagging and the stats built on it: per tag and per combination. More often than not it is not a tag that loses money but its pairing with another one — alone that stays invisible.
landing.section_analytics_body: A lab for selections: set conditions and see how that slice of trades differs from the rest. What matters is not the selection's own number but its distance from the baseline.
landing.section_market_body: The backdrop you traded against: sentiment, volume, positioning, weekday odds. It exists to tell “my system broke” apart from “the market was different”.
landing.keysBody: A read-only key is enough for the journal: with one, even a database leak means an exposed trade history, not a drained account. A Bybit key that can trade also opens the terminal — orders right from the product. Withdrawal permission is never needed. Settings shows what the key allows; key and secret are stored encrypted.
landing.honest1: Live trades have only ever gone through Bybit. The OKX, Bitget, KuCoin, Gate.io, Binance USDⓈ-M and MEXC adapters are written but have not seen a single real trade — their behaviour is unknown, not “fine”.
landing.honest2: Half the value rests on manual tagging. If tagging trades is not something you want to do, this product is not for you — better to learn that now.
landing.honest3: Free for now, no subscription. The product is under active development and its sections change.
landing.endTitle: Start with a dozen tagged trades
landing.endBody: Connect your keys, wait for the sync, tag your recent trades and come back to Overview. Until they are tagged, half the conclusions cannot be drawn.
landing.footer: Trade Play — a crypto futures journal and the stats built on tagging.

onboarding.askBody: A short walkthrough of the product, a couple of minutes. We recommend it now — it won’t offer itself again, but you can always restart it from the profile menu.

overview.welcomeBody: The point of Trade Play is to help you find your trading system and make it stable — to get your trading to where the result repeats instead of depending on luck. Three steps to get there:
overview.welcomeP1Title: Find what actually works for you
overview.welcomeP1Body: You tag why you entered a trade. Trade Play analyzes your trades and shows which setups actually make money, and which only look like they work.
overview.welcomeP2Title: Test it on your own data
overview.welcomeP2Body: Analytics compares a selection matching your conditions against all your other trades. The question it answers is “what if I only traded like this?” — and the answer arrives before you put money behind it.
overview.welcomeP3Body: Edge Score measures not the size of the profit but how repeatable it is. Together with the equity curve, drawdown and profit factor it answers the real question: has the system become steadier or not.
overview.navBody: Overview — what the period came to. Tags — why you entered and how it ended. Analytics — one slice of trades compared against all the rest. Market — the backdrop you traded against. Settings — exchange keys.
overview.periodBody: Everything on this page is counted over the range picked here. Next to it — how many trades fell inside it: when that number is small, treat the conclusions below with care.
overview.summaryBody: Nine numbers for the period. Edge Score rates how repeatable the result is, not how large — it answers "will this hold", not "did this pay". Fees are shown separately and already deducted from PnL.
overview.equityBody: How the result accumulated over time. What matters is the shape of the path, not the final point: a steady climb and the same sum earned in one lucky day after a long drawdown are different systems.
overview.positionsBody: Open positions and the numbers behind them: how long a trade has been running and where in the move the entry was. Tag it straight away, without waiting for the close: with the button in the row, or from the Telegram notification.
overview.tradesBody: This is where the value starts. The tag button in a row is the action everything else is counted for: until trades are tagged, the product knows nothing about them beyond the exchange's numbers. Rows expand — orders, fees and funding are inside.
overview.chartBody: Entry and exit prices are underlined with a dash — clicking either one opens the candles around the trade: the corridor price travelled before the entry, and where inside it your entry sat. That answers “did I take the edge or the middle of the move”, which a single number in the row can't show.
overview.nextBody: If your exchange keys are not connected yet, start with Settings. A read-only key is enough. Then start tagging your trades — and in time you will see the patterns in them.

tags.introBody: A tag is a short label for why you entered: a setup, an emotion or a mistake. Create tags and mark up both your trades and your own strategies with them. The more trades you tag, the clearer it gets which trades make money and which only look like they work.
tags.combosBody: Tag combinations and their results. The "Create" row adds a combination to the table.
tags.allBody: How to read this column matters: a trade counts toward each of its tags IN FULL, it is not split between them. Rows overlap, and the column does not add up to your total PnL — that is not a bug, it is the only way to keep the number meaningful.

analytics.introBody: A laboratory: you set conditions and see how that slice differs from all of your trades. The question this section answers is "what if I had only traded like this?".
analytics.filtersBody: Tags, direction, instrument, timeframe, entry time. Conditions stack: the more of them, the smaller the slice — and the more carefully the result has to be read.
analytics.compareBody: The section's main numbers: the slice on one side, all trades in the period next to it, and the difference between them. It is the difference that answers the question, not the slice's absolute number.
analytics.equityBody: How this part of your trades would have behaved on its own. Empty means fewer than two trades matched the conditions; loosen the filters.

market.introBody: This section is not about your trades but about the backdrop they happened against. It is here so you can tell "the system broke" apart from "the market was different".
market.macroBody: Sentiment, capitalisation, volumes. Broad strokes — enough to know what conditions your period was counted in.
market.positioningBody: How the crowd is placed on the chosen instrument, and what open interest and volatility are doing. Above-normal volatility is flagged separately: that is the case where your usual position size already means a different risk.
market.weekdayBody: How the market behaved by day of week over the chosen history depth. This is the market's statistic, not yours: comparing it with your own breakdown on Overview is the point of the section.

settings.keysBody: A read-only key is enough for the journal: with it, even a leaked database means an exposed trade history, not a drained account. A Bybit key that can trade adds the “Terminal” section — orders to the exchange right from here. A key with any permissions connects, and the “Key permissions” row shows what it allows, as the exchange itself reports; withdrawal permission is never needed.
settings.exchangeBody: Several can be connected, but only one — the active one — is read and synced. An honest warning: live trades have so far only gone through Bybit; how the other adapters behave is unknown.
settings.telegramBody: Link the bot and trade notifications arrive in your chat — you can tag a trade right from there. Which signals are sent is set up here as well.

backtest.introBody: A random slice of BTC history: candles open one at a time, the future is hidden. You enter and exit yourself — the same decision as a real trade, without the real risk.
backtest.sessionsBody: Your runs, newest first. Resume an unfinished one from where you left off; a finished one already shows win rate, total R, and PnL.
backtest.statsBody: A summary across all runs and a breakdown by tag — the same tags you use on real trades. A trade with several tags is counted in full for each one, so the column doesn't add up to the overall total.

NO_EXCHANGE.title: No exchange connected
NO_EXCHANGE.body: The terminal trades on Bybit with your key. Connect a Bybit key that has trading permission.

NOT_BYBIT.title: The terminal works with Bybit only
NOT_BYBIT.body: Another exchange is active right now. Connect Bybit with a key that can trade and make it the active exchange.

READ_ONLY.title: The key can't trade
READ_ONLY.body: The Bybit key is connected read-only: enough for the journal, but the terminal needs order permission (Contract — Orders, Positions). Add it to the key on Bybit or connect another key.

UNKNOWN.title: Couldn't read the key's permissions
UNKNOWN.body: Bybit didn't answer about the key's permissions, and the terminal doesn't open without that answer. Refresh the page a little later.
